doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

chapter: Working with American visitors and moving to the U.S.
title: Leaving Oxford and working with Sandy Brown and Red Allen
summary: After three years at Oxford Ingham went professional against his parents' wishes, played with Sandy Brown, then Henry 'Red' Allen, whose showmanship and New Orleans stories he describes.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well let me get back to — that was wonderful to hear — I want to get back to you started accompanying visiting American jazz musicians?

Yeah. I got lucky. I was so lucky in fact one of my first jobs, well I went to the university, just to please my parents kind of thing, but I wanted to go, you know, it was three good years. I played with university jazz bands there. And when I left it, I was up at Oxford for three years, and I loved it, that was great. But then I thought now I’ve got to do what I want to do. I’ve satisfied them, you know they made sacrifices for me to go the university, okay, that was nice. And I said I’m going to try and do music. And they said oh well it’s a precarious profession, you won’t have a chance, it’s just going to be — he’ll forget about it and go work in a bank later, or do something. Well I’ve been working ever since and kind of never been out of a job. And funny enough, my father, within two years had been made redundant from his steady insurance job, and here is he telling me you’re going to have a precarious kind of situation, and he was kind of scuffling around to try and find something in his middle 50s. So it was kind of ironic. But anyway, when I left the university, yeah, I started playing with local British bands, with wonderful clarinet player who is sadly now dead, Sandy Brown. And then the Americans started to come over that I was talking about. You know, we’re talking about 1964, 5, you know with the start of the British rock thing and the coming over reciprocal arrangements. The first guy, pretty much, that I worked with was Henry “Red” Allen, who was one of the great jazz trumpet players of all time. He’d grown up with the big bands here, Fletcher Henderson, and he’d arrived in New York I guess in about 1927, somewhere around there. And this guy was larger than life. You’re talking not only of a great instrumentalist, and a very original player, but he was also a great showman and a great man for the audience. He would stand there with this wonderful brocade jacket and stand there and talk about his life. He was from New Orleans. His father had had a brass band in New Orleans and he grew up, he knew all the old greats — he knew Jelly Roll Morton, played with Jelly Roll Morton, recorded with Jelly. He knew all the people from New Orleans. He knew Louis Armstrong, of course he knew Sidney Bechet, Albert Nicholas, all these great traditionalists. He was part of that heritage. And he’d get up there and he’d talk to them, you know he’d say, “my father, Henry Allen Senior” he’d say, “Louis Armstrong played for him in his band, and Sidney Bechet.” And then he says, “I was there,” he says, “that was my dad.” And he’d create this spell of magic and then he’d start to play. And you never heard such — a chill. And it was the same kind, the French word I think is frisson you know, that tremor that goes right through you. I got that when I first heard Louis Armstrong live, and it was the All Stars. And the curtains in the theatre are closed © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
